title: Pre-Qin Literature
full_title: Pre-Qin Literature: From Myth to the Masters
tagline: Myths, the *Book of Songs*, its forms and techniques, historical prose, narrative in the *Zuo Zhuan*, the *Analects* and the *Mencius*, Zhuangzi and the other Masters, Qu Yuan and the *Li Sao*, the *Songs of Chu*, and the legacy of early literature
summary: The literature of the centuries before the Qin unification laid foundations that Chinese writers drew on for the next two thousand years. This course reads the early myths, the *Book of Songs*, the historical prose of the *Book of Documents*, the *Zuo Zhuan* and the *Discourses of the States*, the prose of Confucius, Mencius, Zhuangzi and the other Masters, and the poetry of Qu Yuan and the *Songs of Chu*.
overview: Pre-Qin literature is Chinese literature's childhood — and, uncannily, its apprenticeship master: the Book of Songs' four-character odes, the Zuo Zhuan's battle scenes, Mencius' temper, Zhuangzi's fish and butterflies, Qu Yuan's fragrant plants all became the source codes every later dynasty re-encrypted.

This course walks the thousand-year archive by genre and by workshop: mythology's fragments and their Victorian-afterlife reinventions; the Songs' compilation, taxonomy (feng/ya/song), techniques (fu/bi/xing) and music-loss; historical prose from Shangshu's oracles through Spring and Autumn's brush to the Zuo Zhuan's narrative rooms and the Strategies' rhetoric; the Masters' essay society and its argument styles; Qu Yuan inventing the individual voice, the Songs of Chu's shamans, orchids and monster-questions; and finally the twin-inheritance thesis (Feng-Sao) with which later ages explained all literature back to these two shelves.
Prerequisite: Classical Chinese I — every close reading here runs on its six workshop skills (sound, graph, punctuation, syntax, translation, appreciation).
outcomes: map the major pre-Qin corpora (Songs, Documents, Annals, Zuo, Strategies, Analects, Mencius, Zhuangzi, Xunzi, Han Feizi, Chu Ci) to dates, milieus and afterlives
read a 国风 poem with 赋比兴 technique, four-character rhythm and layering, and defend the reading against alternative 美刺 interpretations
analyse Zuo Zhuan battle narratives for their point-of-view control, foreshadowing and diplomatic speech craft
compare the Masters' persuasive styles (Analects' aphorism, Mencius' momentum, Zhuangzi's parable, Han Feizi's edge, Xunzi's architecture)
explain the Chu Ci's shamanic substrate, the 香草美人 allegory's political grammar, and why Liu An called the Li Sao 国风-adjacent
trace 神话 afterlives: how Pangu, Nüwa, Hou Yi and the rest were recorded late, rewritten always, and remain China's most re-told IP
critically use the 风骚并称 template — what it canonized and what it hid
read original-language excerpts (with notes) of each corpus and place scholarly controversies (毛郑异同, 今古文, authorship of Li Sao) at their proper confidence

chapters.title: Myths
chapters.summary: The fragmentary myths of ancient China — Nüwa, Pangu, Kuafu, Jingwei — where they are recorded, and why they survive only in pieces.

chapters.title: The *Book of Songs*
chapters.summary: The 305 poems, how the anthology was compiled, its Airs, Odes and Hymns, and how it became a Confucian classic.

chapters.title: Form and technique in the *Book of Songs*
chapters.summary: Four-character lines, repetition across stanzas, and the techniques of *fu*, *bi* and *xing*.

chapters.title: Historical prose
chapters.summary: The *Book of Documents*, the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, the *Zuo Zhuan*, the *Discourses of the States* and the *Intrigues of the Warring States*.

chapters.title: Narrative in the *Zuo Zhuan*
chapters.summary: How the *Zuo Zhuan* tells of battles, speeches and people, and its influence on later historical writing.

chapters.title: The *Analects* and the *Mencius*
chapters.summary: Recorded sayings and argument: the style of the *Analects* and the persuasive prose of Mencius.

chapters.title: Zhuangzi and the other Masters
chapters.summary: The parables of Zhuangzi, the essays of Xunzi and Han Feizi, and the Mohists and other schools as literature.

chapters.title: Qu Yuan and the *Li Sao*
chapters.summary: Qu Yuan’s life and the *Li Sao*: its fragrant plants and fair ones, its journeys among the gods, and its place in Chinese culture.

chapters.title: The *Songs of Chu*
chapters.summary: The *Nine Songs*, the *Heavenly Questions* and other pieces, the culture of Chu, and how the *Chuci* differ from the *Book of Songs*.

chapters.title: The legacy of pre-Qin literature
chapters.summary: The *Book of Songs* and the *Songs of Chu* as the two sources of Chinese poetry, the traditions of prose founded in this period, and how later writers read them.

history.title: Zhou airs enter their making
history.detail: Western Zhou collection and shaping of airs begins (the “wooden bell on the road” folk-survey is a later legend); the ritual odes of Zhou and the Southern airs reach stable written form.

history.title: Quoting the Oes as diplomacy
history.detail: In the Zuo Zhuan's missions, envoys 赋诗言志 — reciting odes to state what they will not say outright; the anthology becomes the international language of the age and canon by usage.

history.title: Confucius sorts the canon (tradition)
history.detail: “Set the Odes, order the Documents, return the Ya and Song” — whether he deleted or simply taught, the tradition of a Confucian-edited classic fixes the Songs' afterlife as scripture of statecraft and self-cultivation.

history.title: Zuo Zhuan takes written shape
history.detail: The narrative commentary (attributed to Zuo Qiuming) reaches the form we read: battles told in stage-shots, speeches as engine rooms of fate — historical prose matures into literature.

history.title: The essay society
history.detail: Hundred-schools prose in full tilt: Mencius harangues, Zhuangzi parables, Han Feizi files his blades — argument becomes a literary genre with styles of its own.

history.title: First signed voice
history.detail: Qu Yuan composes the Li Sao (traditional dating): the longest poem before the Han, the first great poem with a name behind its grief — the individual enters Chinese literature.

history.title: The last great compilation
history.detail: Lu Buwei's guests compile the Lüshi Chunqiu, claiming to hold all the principles of heaven and earth in one index — the hundred schools close with a systematic table of contents of themselves.

history.title: The burning begins the end
history.detail: Li Si's book-burning edict (excepting medicine, divination, planted records and博士-held copies) closes the pre-Qin era: what survives was preserved by memory, hiding and Han recopying — the first great editorial trauma of the canon.

references.title: 《诗经》
references.note: The source shelf; read with 毛传郑笺 and 朱熹《诗集传》; modern selections from 余冠英 onward.

references.title: 《春秋左氏传》
references.note: Narrative headquarters of early prose; Yang Bojun's 译注 remains the desk standard.

references.title: 《史记·屈原贾生列传》
references.note: The founding biography of Qu Yuan — source and legend at once; every Li Sao dating argument passes through it.

references.title: 《文心雕龙》(《辨骚》《明诗》)
references.note: The first systematic critic's verdict on Feng and Sao — the canonization under audit.

references.title: 《四库全书总目提要》(集·楚词等部)
references.note: Qing official scholarship's map of the pre-Qin holdings —辨章学术,考镜源流 in one shelf.

references.title: 《中国文学史稿》
references.note: The modern survey era's early synthesis — how the twentieth century learned to narrate these texts as literature.
